source_text: Talia quaedam de repromissionibus divinis credimus sentienda, cum intellegentiam nostram ad contemplationem aeterni illius et nullo fine elaudendi saeculi iaculamur atque ineffabilem eius laetitiam ae beatitudinem contemplamur. Verum quoniam in ecclesiastica praedicatione inest etiam de futuro ‚15 dei (iusto) iudicio fides, quae iudieii eredulitas provocat homines et suadet ad bene beateque vivendum et omni genere refugere peccatum, et per hoc sine dubio indieatur quod in nostra sit positum potestate vel laudabili nos vitae vel culpabili dedere: propterea necessarium reor pauca etiam de arbitrii nostri libertate disserere, eo quod non ignobiliter (20 haee quoque quaestio a quam plurimis agitetur. Ut autem facilius quid sit libertas arbitrii cognoscamus, quid sibi velit natura ipsius arbitrii voluntatisque requiramus. 2. Omnium quae moventur alia in semet ipsis causas motuum suorum gerunt, alia extrinsecus accipiunt: ut puta extrinsecus tantummodo moventur omnia, quae sine vita sunt, ut lapides vel ligna et quaeeumque huiusmodi sunt, quae solo habitu materiae suae vel corporum constant. Omittenda sane nune est illa quaestio, quae etiam illum motum putat esse, cum per corruptelam corpora dissolvuntur; nihil enim nunc haee ad propositum conducunt. Alia vero in semet ipsis habent movendi causam, ut animalia vel arbores et omnia, quae vel per naturalem vitam vel per animam constant; inter quae etiam metallorum venas deputari aliquibus visum est, sed et ignis sui motus esse putandus est, fortassis autem etiam fontes aquarum. Haec autem, quae in semet ipsis causam suorum motuum habent, quaedam dieunt ex se, quaedam ab se moveri; et ita dividunt quod ex se moveantur ea, quae vivunt quidem non tamen animantia sunt, a se autem moveantur animantia, cum eis fantasia, id est voluntas quaedam vel incitamentum, adfuerit, quae ea moveri ad aliquid vel incitari provocaverit. Denique etiam in quibusdam animalibus inest talis fantasia, id est voluntas vel sensus, qui ea natural quodam instinctu provocet et concitet ad ordinatos et conpositos motus; sieut videmus araneas facere, quae fantasia, id est voluntate quadam vel studio textrinae, ad opus texendi ordinatissime concitantur, sine dubio naturali quodam motu intentionem huiuscemodi operis provocante, nec tamen ultra alium ahquem sensum quam texendi naturale studium habere ipsum animal invenitur, sicut et apis fingendi favos ac mella, ut aiunt, aöria congre3. Rationabile vero animal cum habeat in se et hos naturales motus, habet tamen amplius ceteris animalibus etiam rationis vim, qua ludicare et discernere de motibus naturalibus possit et alios quidem reprobare et abicere alios vero probare atque suscipere, cuius rationis iudicio dirigi et gubernari hominis motus ad vitam probabilem possint. Unde consequens est ut, quoniam natura rationis huius, quae est in homine, habet in se vim dinoscendi boni vel mali, idque cum discreverit, inest ei facultas etiam eligendi quod probaverit, in eligendo quidem quod bonum est laudabilis, in sequendo vero quod turpe vel malum est iure culpabilis iudicetur. Illud sane nequaquam latere nos debet, quod in nonnullis mutis animalibus ordinatior quidam motus a ceteris animalibus invenitur, ut in sagacibus canibus vel bellatoribus equis, ita ut videantur aliquibus velut rationabili quodam sensu moveri; sed id non tam ratione quam incentivo quodam et naturah motu, pro huiuscemodi usibus largius indulto, fieri credendum est. Verum ut dieere eoeperamus, cum ita se habeat rationabile animal, nobis hominibus incidere quidem extrinsecus possunt aliqua et occurrere sive ad visum sive ad auditum vel ad alios sensus, quae nos concitent ac provocent ad bonos vel contrarios motus;
pass_a_gloss: We believe that certain things about divine promises are to be understood, when we throw our understanding to the contemplation of that eternal and endless praise of the age, and we contemplate its ineffable joy and beatitude. But since in ecclesiastical preaching there is also faith about the future judgment of God, which provokes the credibility of judgment and persuades men to live well and blessedly and to flee from all kinds of sin, and through this it is undoubtedly indicated that it is in our power to give ourselves to a praiseworthy or culpable life: therefore I think it is necessary to discuss also a few things about the freedom of our will, because this question is also being discussed by very many people, not without nobility. So that we may more easily know what the freedom of will is, let us investigate what the nature of will itself means. Of all things that are moved, some have the causes of their movements within themselves, others receive them from outside: as, for example, all things that are without life are moved only from outside, such as stones or wood and whatever things of this kind are, which consist only in the condition of their matter or bodies. Indeed, that question which also thinks that movement is when bodies are dissolved through corruption, is to be omitted now, for it does not contribute to the present purpose. But other things have the cause of movement within themselves, such as animals or trees and all things that consist either through natural life or through a soul; among which some people have also thought that the veins of metals should be counted, and also the movement of fire is to be thought, and perhaps also the springs of water. But these things, which have the cause of their movements within themselves, some are said to move from themselves, some from themselves; and thus they divide that they move from themselves, those that live, indeed, but are not animate, from themselves, however, animate things move, when fantasy, that is, a certain will or incitement, is present, which has provoked and incited them to move or to be incited to something. Finally, even in certain animals there is such a fantasy, that is, a will or sense, which provokes and incites them by a certain natural instinct to ordered and composed movements; as we see spiders doing, which are incited to the work of weaving in a very orderly way by a certain fantasy, that is, by a certain will or zeal for weaving, without doubt, a natural movement provoking the intention of this work, and yet the animal itself is not found to have any other sense than the natural zeal for weaving, just as the bee is said to make honeycombs and honey from the air. But the rational animal, since it has within itself also these natural movements, has, however, more than the other animals also the power of reason, by which it can judge and discern about natural movements and reject and cast away some, and approve and accept others, by the judgment of which reason the movements of man can be directed and governed to a probable life. Whence it follows that, since the nature of this reason, which is in man, has within itself the power of distinguishing good or evil, and when it has discerned, there is also the faculty of choosing what it has approved, in choosing, indeed, what is good, it is praiseworthy, in following, however, what is base or evil, it is justly culpable. Indeed, it should not escape our notice that in some mute animals a more ordered movement is found than in other animals, such as in keen dogs or war horses, so that they seem to be moved by a certain rational sense; but this is to be believed to happen not so much by reason as by a certain incitement and natural movement, more abundantly given for such uses. But as we began to say, since the rational animal is such, certain things can happen to us humans from outside and occur, either to sight or to hearing or to other senses, which provoke and incite us to good or contrary movements;

choices.why: verb meaning to throw or direct
noun meaning a long period of time
gerund meaning the act of praising

pass_b_english: We hold that certain matters concerning divine promises are to be understood when we cast our understanding toward the contemplation of that eternal age which admits no end of praise, and when we contemplate its ineffable joy and blessedness.

Yet because ecclesiastical preaching also contains faith in the future judgment of God, and because the credibility of that judgment stirs people and urges them to live well and blessedly and to flee every kind of sin, and because this unmistakably shows that it lies in our power to hand ourselves over either to a praiseworthy life or to a culpable one, I consider it necessary to discuss a few things about the freedom of our will, since this question, too, is agitated by very many people not without dignity.
In order that we may more readily grasp what freedom of will is, let us inquire what the nature of will itself intends.
Of all things that are moved, some carry the causes of their movements within themselves, while others receive them from outside.
For example, all things that lack life are moved only from outside, such as stones or wood and whatever things of that sort there are, which consist solely in the condition of their matter or bodies.
We must set aside for now the question that even regards dissolution through corruption as movement, because it contributes nothing to the present purpose.
Other things, however, possess the cause of movement within themselves, such as animals or trees and all things that subsist either through natural life or through a soul.
Among these, some have thought that veins of metal should be counted, and fire too is to be regarded as having its own movement, and perhaps also the springs of water.

Now those things which have the cause of their movements within themselves, some are said to move from themselves, some from themselves; and so they distinguish things that move from themselves, which live indeed but are not animate, from things that move from themselves, namely animate beings, when fantasy, that is, a certain will or incitement, is present which has provoked and incited them to move or to be incited to something.
Finally, even in certain animals there is such a fantasy, that is, a will or sense, which by a certain natural instinct provokes and incites them to ordered and composed movements.

We see this in spiders, which are incited to the work of weaving in a most orderly way by a certain fantasy, that is, by a certain will or zeal for weaving, a natural movement undoubtedly provoking the intention of such a work, and yet the animal itself is found to have no other sense than the natural zeal for weaving, just as the bee is said to fashion honeycombs and honey from the air.

The rational animal, since it has these natural movements within itself, nevertheless possesses something more than the other animals, namely the power of reason, by which it can judge and discern concerning natural movements and reject and cast away some, and approve and accept others, so that by the judgment of this reason the movements of a human being can be directed and governed toward a praiseworthy life.

From this it follows that, since the nature of this reason which is in a human being has within itself the power of distinguishing good or evil, and once it has discerned, there is also present in it the faculty of choosing what it has approved; in choosing what is good it is praiseworthy, but in following what is base or evil it is justly judged culpable.

It should by no means escape our notice that in some mute animals a more ordered movement is found than in other animals, such as in keen dogs or warhorses, so that they appear to be moved by a certain rational sense; but this is to be believed to happen not so much by reason as by a certain incitement and natural movement, more abundantly granted for such uses.

But as we began to say, since the rational animal is such, certain things can befall us humans from outside and present themselves, whether to sight or to hearing or to other senses, which provoke and incite us to good or contrary movements.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances of the Latin (e.g., 'not without dignity' for 'non ignobiliter', 'justly judged culpable' for 'iure culpabilis iudicetur'). All clauses, including the complex distinctions regarding animal movement and the role of 'fantasia', are preserved.
